entries.meaning: Daśaratha bows to every sage, worships them lovingly and gives fine seats. Four hundred thousand gentle cows, splendid as wish-fulfilling Surabhi, are fully ornamented and presented to the Brahmins. The king humbly says he has gained the fruit of human life that day, then calls the petitioners and gives gold, clothing, jewels, horses, elephants and chariots according to each taste. They leave singing victory to the lord of the solar line. Bowing repeatedly at Kauśika’s feet, Daśaratha says all this happiness is the gift of the sage’s gracious glance.

Daśaratha praises Janaka’s affection, character, deeds and magnificence. Each morning he asks leave to return to Ayodhyā, but Janaka lovingly detains him with ever-renewed honour and thousands of forms of hospitality. Many days pass as though the guests were bound by a cord of affection, and no one in the joyful city wants Daśaratha to go. At last Kauśika and Śatānanda counsel Janaka to permit the departure, though he can scarcely relinquish love. Janaka summons his ministers, who bow but become speechless with feeling when told to announce the king’s intention.

The townspeople hear that the procession will leave and anxiously question one another; once the news is certain they droop like lotuses at dusk. Along the return route Janaka sends abundant stores of dried fruit, prepared food and every provision. He gives one hundred thousand horses, twenty-five thousand chariots, ten thousand splendid rutting elephants, and loads of gold, clothing, gems, buffaloes, cows and many other goods. The immeasurable dowry makes the wealth of the world-guardians seem slight.

Hearing the wedding party will leave, all the queens become distressed like fish in dwindling water. Again and again they take Sītā into their laps, bless and instruct her: remain forever dear to your husband, may your married fortune endure, serve parents-in-law and guru, attend to your husband’s disposition and follow his wishes. Wise friends softly teach the duties of a wife; the queens counsel every princess, repeatedly clasp them to the heart, and lament why Brahmā created women for such partings. At that moment Rāma and his brothers come to Janaka’s palace to take leave.

All four naturally lovely brothers draw the city’s men and women, who urge one another to fill their eyes with the dear young royal guests before Janaka sends them away. They wonder what past merit has brought such a vision: it is like nectar to the dying, a wish-tree to one hungry from birth, or Hari’s abode to a soul in hell. They tell each other to enshrine Rāma’s beauty in the heart as a serpent bears its crest-jewel. Giving every eye its reward, the princes reach the palace; the women’s quarters rise in delight to behold the ocean-like beauty of all four brothers and perform lamps and offerings.

The mothers-in-law gaze at Rāma with intense love, repeatedly fall at his feet, bathe the brothers after ceremonial unction, and feed them lovingly with all six flavours. At the right moment Rāma gently says that Daśaratha wishes to leave for Ayodhyā and has sent them to take leave; he asks the joyful mothers to grant permission and continue loving them as children. The whole women’s palace breaks into tears and the mothers cannot answer. They clasp all the princesses and, with many entreaties, entrust each bride to her husband.

The queen remains holding Rāma’s feet, her speech submerged in the mud of love. Hearing words steeped in affection, Rāma honours his mother-in-law in many ways, joins his hands for leave, bows repeatedly, receives her blessing, and departs with his brothers. The queens grow weak as they hold his sweet form in their hearts, then summon the princesses once more. Mothers and daughters meet, part, turn back and embrace again until the wise friends separate them like cows led away from their calves. Compassion and separation seem to have made their dwelling throughout Videha’s palace.

Sītā’s parrots and mynahs, born and trained in golden cages, cry distractedly, ‘Where is Vaidehī?’ Their calls destroy everyone’s composure; if birds and beasts suffer so, human grief cannot be told. Janaka arrives with the family, eyes flooding as love surges. At sight of Sītā the firmness for which the great renunciant is famed deserts him: he draws Jānakī to his breast and the lofty restraint of knowledge dissolves. Wise ministers attempt consolation but recognize the moment is not receptive. He embraces his daughter repeatedly, orders beautiful palanquins, and remembers the divine powers and Gaṇeśa before seating the princesses.

Janaka counsels his daughter in many ways and teaches women’s duties and family custom. He gives many pure servants dear to Sītā. As she departs, the townspeople are distraught even while auspicious signs abound. The king, Brahmins, ministers and court accompany the party; at the proper moment instruments sound and chariots, elephants and horses are readied. Daśaratha summons and fully honours the Brahmins with gifts, places their lotus-foot dust upon his head, receives blessings, remembers Gaṇeśa, and starts for Ayodhyā amid flowers, celestial songs and resounding drums.

Janaka respectfully turns back the leading citizens and gives every petitioner ornaments, garments, horses and elephants, nourishing them with love. They recite praises and return with Rāma in their hearts. Daśaratha repeatedly asks his fellow king to turn home, but Janaka cannot bring himself to leave; at last the lord of Kosala descends and stands beside him, tears swelling in both kings’ eyes. Videha joins his hands and says words steeped in the nectar of affection, unable to devise a courtesy adequate to the great honour Daśaratha has bestowed. Their humility and mutual love overflow the heart.
